title: The mills of the gods and the justice of God
source_text: Καὶ ἡμεῖς μὲν ὅ τι ποτὲ περὶ κολάσεως λέγοντες καὶ διὰ τῆς περὶ κολάσεως διδασκαλίας πολλοὺς ἀπὸ τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων ἐπιστρέφομεν· ὁ δὲ κατὰ τὸν Κέλσον ἱερεὺς τοῦ Ἀπόλλωνος ἢ τοῦ Διὸς οἷα ἀποκρίνεται, κατανοήσωμεν· ὀψὲ, φησὶ, θεῶν ἀλέουσι μύλοι, καὶ ἐς παίδων παῖδας, τοί κεν μετόπισθε γένωνται. ὅρα δὲ ὅσῳ τούτου βέλτιον τὸ „οὐκ ἀποθανοῦνται πατέρες ὑπὲρ τέκνων, οὐδὲ υἱοὶ ἀποθανοῦνται ὑπὲρ πατέρων· ἕκαστος τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ἑαυτοῦ ἀποθανεῖται“ καὶ τοῦτο „τοῦ φαγόντος τὸν ὄμφακα αἱμωδιάσουσιν οἱ ὀδόντες αὐτοῦ“ καὶ τὸ „υἱὸς οὐ λήψεται ἀδικίαν πατρὸς, καὶ πατὴρ οὐ λήψεται ἀδικίαν υἱοῦ· δικαιοσύνη δικαίου ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸν ἔσται, καὶ ἀνομία ἀνόμου ἐπ᾿ αὐτὸν ἔσται.“ ἐὰν δέ τις ὅμοιον εἶναι λέγῃ τῷ ἐς παίδων παῖδας, τοί κεν μετόπισθε γένωνται τὸ „ἀποδιδοὺς ἁμαρτίας πατέρων ἐπὶ τέκνα ἐπὶ τρίτην καὶ τετάρτην γενεὰν τοῖς μισοῦσί (με) ,“ μαθέτω ὅτι ἐν τῷ Ἰεζεκιὴλ „παραβολὴ“ τὸ τοιοῦτον εἶναι λέλεκται, αἰτιωμένῳ τοὺς λέγοντας· „οἱ πατέρες ἔφαγον ὄμφακα, καὶ οἱ ὀδόντες τῶν τέκνων ᾑμωδίασαν,“ ᾧ ἐπιφέρεται· „ζῶ ἐγὼ, λέγει κύριος,“ „ἀλλ᾿ ἢ ἕκαστος τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ἁμαρτίᾳ ἀποθανεῖται.“ οὐ κατὰ τὸν παρόντα δὲ καιρόν ἐστι διηγήσασθαι, τί σημαίνει ἡ περὶ τοῦ „ (ἐπὶ) τρίτην καὶ τετάρτην γενεὰν“ ἀποδίδοσθαι τὰς „ἁμαρτίας“ παραβολή.
pass_a_gloss: And we, whatever we say about punishment (κόλασις), also through the teaching (διδασκαλία) about punishment turn (ἐπιστρέφω) many from sins (ἁμάρτημα); but the priest (ἱερεύς) of Apollo or Zeus according to Celsus, what sort of things he answers (ἀποκρίνομαι), let us consider: 'late (ὀψέ),' he says, 'grind (ἀλέω) the mills (μύλοι) of the gods, even to children's children (παίδων παῖδες), who may be born after (μετόπισθε).' See how much better than this is: 'fathers will not die for children, nor will sons die for fathers; each will die by his own sin (ἁμαρτία)' and this: 'of the one who ate the unripe grape (ὄμφαξ) the teeth will be set on edge (αἱμωδιάω)' and 'a son will not take (λαμβάνω) the injustice (ἀδικία) of a father, and a father will not take the injustice of a son; righteousness (δικαιοσύνη) of the righteous will be upon him, and lawlessness (ἀνομία) of the lawless will be upon him.' But if someone says that like 'to children's children, who may be born after' is 'repaying (ἀποδίδωμι) sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation (γενεά) to those hating (μισέω) me,' let him learn that in Ezekiel such a thing has been said to be a 'parable (παραβολή),' [Ezekiel] blaming (αἰτιάομαι) those saying: 'the fathers ate unripe grape, and the teeth of the children were set on edge,' to which is added (ἐπιφέρω): 'I live, says the Lord,' 'but rather each will die by his own sin.' It is not according to the present occasion (καιρός) to narrate what the parable about the sins being repaid to the third and fourth generation signifies (σημαίνω).
pass_b_english: We, for our part, whatever we may say about punishment, do turn many from their sins through the teaching about punishment. But let us consider what sort of answer the priest of Apollo or of Zeus gives in Celsus’s account: “Late,” he says, “grind the mills of the gods, even to children’s children, who may be born later.”

See how much better than this are the words, “Fathers shall not die for children, nor shall sons die for fathers; each shall die for his own sin” (Deuteronomy 24:16), and this, “The one who ate the sour grape shall have his teeth set on edge” (Jeremiah 31:30), and this, “A son shall not bear the unrighteousness of his father, and a father shall not bear the unrighteousness of his son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the lawlessness of the lawless shall be upon him” (Ezekiel 18:20).

But if anyone says that the words, “repaying the sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me” (Deuteronomy 5:9; compare Exodus 20:5), are like “to children’s children, who may be born later,” let him learn that in Ezekiel such a saying is called a “parable” (Ezekiel 18:2–3), where the prophet blames those who say, “The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge” (Ezekiel 18:2; compare Jeremiah 31:29), and to this is added, “As I live, says the Lord” (Ezekiel 18:3), “but each shall die for his own sin” (Jeremiah 31:30). This is not the right time to explain what the parable means about “sins” being repaid “to the third and fourth generation.”

choices.choice: The priest’s verses are Celsus’s quotation (Celsus’s words in double quotation marks). ‘Late grind the mills of the gods’ is a proverbial line also found in Sextus Empiricus (Against the Mathematicians 1.287); the second line is close to Homer, Iliad 20.308 (‘and children’s children, who are born after’); not cited inline because the exact source of the combined oracle is uncertain. Jeremiah 31:30 = LXX Jeremiah 38:30. The wording ‘upon children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me’ matches LXX Deuteronomy 5:9 most closely; Exodus 20:5 (and Exodus 34:7) carry the same saying, so Exodus 20:5 is listed in bible_refs. ‘Parable’ comes from Ezekiel 18:3 (ἡ παραβολὴ αὕτη), whose proverb is quoted from Ezekiel 18:2. Origen joins ‘As I live, says the Lord’ (Ezekiel 18:3) to ‘but each shall die in his own sin’, which is the wording of LXX Jeremiah 38:30 (English 31:30), with Ezekiel 18:4 giving the same sense; cited as Jeremiah 31:30. (ἐπὶ) and (με) are Koetschau’s supplements, followed. ὄμφαξ rendered ‘sour grape’ (unripe grape). Reviewer: παραβολή stands in both Ezekiel 18:2 and 18:3 (LXX), so ‘parable’ is cited Ezekiel 18:2–3. Origen’s wording of the proverb (ᾑμωδίασαν) matches LXX Jeremiah 38:29 (English 31:29); LXX Ezekiel 18:2 has ἐγομφίασαν, hence ‘compare Jeremiah 31:29’. The same Greek τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ἁμαρτίᾳ ἀποθανεῖται is now rendered ‘die for his own sin’ in both places.
opening: restored μέν/καί ('We, for our part, whatever we may say about punishment, do turn many')
oracle line 'who are born after them' -> 'who may be born later' (κεν + subjunctive; no added 'them'), in both places
Jeremiah 31:30 calque 'He who ate ..., his teeth shall' -> 'The one who ate the sour grape shall have his teeth set on edge'
'For the prophet blames' -> 'where the prophet blames' (αἰτιωμένῳ is circumstantial, not causal)
'die in his own sin' -> 'die for his own sin' to match the identical Greek in Deuteronomy 24:16
citations: Deuteronomy 5:9 + 'compare Exodus 20:5'; 'parable' -> Ezekiel 18:2–3; proverb -> 'Ezekiel 18:2; compare Jeremiah 31:29'
